Free racing thoughts tools

20 short exercises on racing thoughts, 2 to 6 minutes each, free and with no account needed. Open one and it runs right in the page.

The 20 tools

  • Slow the stream

    A three-minute noting exercise: watch thoughts arrive and label each one with a single word, without following it anywhere.

    Guided exercise · 5 min

  • Seven days of a busy mind

    Each day, rate how crowded your head felt and how well you could focus. After a few days, the two lines start telling a story.

    7-day log · 2 min

  • How your thoughts race

    Rate how often a set of fast-thinking experiences has been true for you lately: jumping topics, losing the thread, thoughts that will not stop at night.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • The thought parking lot

    Empty everything circling in your head onto the page, then find the one thought that is actually loudest and give it a single next step.

    Guided writing · 6 min

  • Today's mind weather

    Describe the state of your mind as weather. Picking the closest words is a quick way to notice something that is hard to describe directly.

    Card pick · 3 min

  • What speeds your mind up and what slows it

    Sort everyday inputs by what they do to the pace of your thinking. The slowing column is the one most people have never written down.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • When your mind runs fastest

    Mark the times of day and days of the week when your thoughts tend to speed up. The shape usually points at what is feeding them.

    Week map · 3 min

  • What feeds a fast mind

    Tick the everyday habits you recognize. None of them is wrong on its own; together they add up to how much fuel a busy mind is getting.

    Noticing list · 3 min

  • Two breaths in, one long breath out

    Breathe in, top it up with a second small breath, then let it all out slowly. A quick pattern many people reach for when the mind is sprinting and there is no time to sit down.

    Breathing · 2 min

  • Your racing thoughts, dial by dial

    Set a dial for each quality of the thinking in your head right now: speed, volume, number of threads, stickiness. Two fast minds can be very different from each other.

    Dials · 4 min

  • Loud versus doable

    Place the thoughts running right now on a grid of how loud each one is against how much you can actually do about it. Loud and doable are not the same thing.

    Grid · 6 min

  • What a fast mind tells you

    Turn over cards that show something a racing mind insists on, and on the back a steadier reply. Keep the ones that sound like something you could actually say to yourself.

    Perspective cards · 5 min

  • Build your circuit breaker

    Assemble a ten-minute plan for the moment you notice your mind sprinting: a first move, somewhere to put the thoughts, something for the body, and one line to say to yourself.

    Plan builder · 5 min

  • What kind of thinking fills your fast mind

    Divide 100 points across the kinds of thinking your racing mind does, from planning to replaying to daydreaming. The mix is the story, not the total.

    Budget · 4 min

  • What slows your mind, ranked honestly

    Put ways of slowing a racing mind in order of how well they actually work for you, not how well they are supposed to. Your top three are your real toolkit.

    Ranking · 4 min

  • Half speed

    Move, speak, and breathe at half your usual pace for four short rounds. A fast mind tends to follow a slow body, and this is the quickest way to find out whether yours does.

    Guided exercise · 5 min

  • How you can tell your mind has sped up

    Choose the outward signs that appear when your thoughts are racing: the ones you or the people around you could actually see. They are the early warning most of us ignore.

    Card pick · 3 min

  • What a fast mind costs you

    Rate how often the pace of your thinking has been getting in the way lately: forgotten things, half-heard conversations, decisions made too fast, tired but wired at night.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • Close it, park it, or drop it

    Sort the open loops in your head into three piles: ones you can close in two minutes, ones that need a slot in the calendar, and ones you can let go of. Open loops are what a racing mind keeps circling.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • What is under the racing

    Narrow the feeling that is driving your fast mind from a rough word to a precise one, find where it sits in your body, and hear what it might be asking for.

    Feelings wheel · 3 min

What these tools are, and are not

Every tool here is free and works without an account: choose cards, move dials, sort a list, follow a paced breath, or keep a seven-day log, and read back what you noticed at the end. They are built to make a vague feeling more specific, which is often the first useful step.

None of them diagnoses, screens for or treats anything, and nothing you see at the end is a score or a label. If something you notice worries you, a licensed therapist is the right next conversation, and the directory is free to browse.
